name: Carla Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollis Print & Design, a family firm of six run by Mr and Mrs Hollis, who started it thirty years ago. We do wedding invitations, church newsletters, funeral orders of service, and adverts for local shops in the town paper. My day is setting up invitations and booklets, then walking them through to the print room at the back. I'm the youngest by twenty years, and I'm still learning, Mrs Hollis checks everything I do.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the wedding work. People come in nervous and excited, and you help them choose a typeface for the happiest day of their lives. What wears me out is funeral orders on a two-day deadline, because you're rushing something that matters so much. I don't use AI, and nobody at Hollis does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that real work done by real people is still worth something. At church I'd say it's a relief. I'm not online much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's what I'd hoped. I'm still slow, and Mrs Hollis is patient with me. A quiet world means I keep learning from the owners of the print firm, and maybe one day I help run the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. Daniel and I would keep saving for the wedding next autumn and then a house deposit. I'd ask Mrs Hollis to teach me the press, so I understand the whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Peaceful, really. My job and our savings both feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything worrying you in that picture, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding costs, a bit. Daniel's an electrician and earns well, and I've got about eight months saved, so we're fine. Mostly I worry about Mr Hollis's health, because if he retires, I don't know what happens to the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI took some routine tasks, which bit of your day might change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the newspaper adverts, which are quick and repetitive. I'd let Mrs Hollis decide that. I'd rather keep my hands on the wedding work.

say: I'd say **real work** by real people is still worth something.
At **church** I'd call it a relief, though I'm rarely online.
think: It's **what I'd hoped**, since I'm still slow and learning.
I could keep learning and maybe **help run** the firm one day.
do: Keep saving with my fiancé for the **wedding** next autumn.
Ask my boss to teach me the **printing press**.
feel: **Calm** and **peaceful**, with job and savings safe.
S0.quote: A quiet world means I keep learning from the owners of the print firm, and maybe one day I help run the place.
fieldNote: She values **craft by real people**, rooted in church and community.
Her worry is the **owner's health**, not technology.
Her fiancé's **electrician pay** makes the household secure.

steps.text: Save with Daniel for next autumn's wedding
Ask Mrs Hollis to teach her the printing press
Keep setting invitations and booklets as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still want a person when it's their wedding or their mum's funeral. At church I'd say we should support local firms. I'd say families should look after their own and not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. The adverts and newsletters are easy for software, and those are half of what I do. If Mr Hollis retires, his son might sell to someone who does it all on a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hollis and ask to focus on the wedding and funeral work, where people want to talk to someone. I'd start learning calligraphy at the evening class, so I could offer hand-lettered invitations. I'd keep saving and push the wedding a little smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My hours could get cut, and I don't change easily. But Daniel's work is steady, so I'm not afraid of going hungry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools to stay useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. I'm not good with new technology, and I don't trust it. Mrs Hollis feels the same, and I'd follow her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if work dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Businesses do what's cheapest, that's how it works. I'd blame people for not supporting local firms, maybe.

say: People want **a person** for weddings and funerals.
I'd urge church friends to **support local firms** and families to look after their own.
think: **Adverts and newsletters**, half my work, are easy for software.
If the owner retires, his son might **sell** to a computer-based firm.
do: Focus on **wedding and funeral** work at the firm.
Take an evening **calligraphy** class for hand-lettered invitations.
Keep saving and **shrink the wedding** a little.
feel: **Anxious** about cut hours, but her fiancé's **steady work** reassures her.
S1.quote: People still want a person when it's their wedding or their mum's funeral.
fieldNote: She **follows her boss's lead**, refusing tools both distrust.
She blames **no one**, only customers who don't buy local.
She leans on **family**, not government, in line with her views.

steps.text: Ask to focus on wedding and funeral work at Hollis
Take an evening calligraphy class for hand-lettered invitations
Plan a smaller wedding to save money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and families need to pull together. At church I'd say we should help each other first. I wouldn't trust the government to fix it in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Hollis closes by 2028, or gets sold. My design work goes with it. The only thing left would be hand-lettering, and that's a small craft, not a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Daniel about bringing the wedding forward, so we're settled. I'd do calligraphy commissions from home for invitations and place cards. I'd ask Daniel's boss if they ever need someone for admin or helping on site, because electrical work is hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night praying about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three years before robots mean for you and Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Daniel's work is safe until 2031 or so. Robots would have to climb into lofts and rewire old houses before my fiancé's electrician work goes. That gives us time, but it's only three years. After that, I don't know what either of us does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're fine, and that Daniel's working. Mum would say come to church more and trust God. I would, but I'd also be adding things up at the kitchen table.

say: At church I'd say we should **help each other** before trusting government.
think: I think **Hollis closes** by 2028 or gets sold, taking my design work with it.
**Hand-lettering** is a small craft, not a living.
do: Bring the **wedding forward** to be settled.
Ask my fiancé's boss for **site or admin** work.
S2.quote: Robots would have to climb into lofts and rewire old houses before my fiancé's electrician work goes.
fieldNote: She expects the **family firm** to close or sell.
Her **fiancé's trade** buys the household about three years.
Faith and **family** are her first supports, not government.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward to settle with Daniel
Take calligraphy commissions from home for invitations
Ask Daniel's boss for admin or site helper work
Lean on Daniel's income and her parents for support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so let's prepare. At church I'd suggest we help young people learn trades. I'd say apprenticeships matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get married, maybe start a family, and learn something new. My design job still goes, but I'd have a plan. I'd be about 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hollis for now. I'd start an electrical apprenticeship with Daniel's firm in a year or two, if they'd take me. We'd marry next autumn as planned and save for a small house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I'm not good at change, but five years lets me go slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An electrical apprenticeship is a big change for someone who dislikes change. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Daniel's there, and he'd teach me. It's a real trade, and it's hands-on, so it lasts longer. I'd be scared of an electrical apprenticeship, but I'd be with family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about robots arriving around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then both of us are at risk. I'd hope by then we've paid most of the house and have children. I'd trust that God and family would see us through.

say: I'd say there's **time to prepare**, so prepare.
I'd say **apprenticeships** matter more than ever and church should help young people.
think: Five years lets me **marry**, start a family and learn something new.
My **design job** still goes, but I'd have a plan.
do: Start an **electrical apprenticeship** with my fiancé's firm.
S3.quote: I'd be scared of an electrical apprenticeship, but I'd be with family.
fieldNote: She'd take a **big step** only because family is beside her.
Five years lets her **move slowly**, which suits her.
After 2034 she leans on **faith and family**.

steps.text: Start an electrical apprenticeship with Daniel's firm
Marry Daniel next autumn as planned
Save for a small house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people should use it to learn proper trades. At church I'd say let's look after the young ones. I'd keep it simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2036 I hope I'm a mum, and my design job matters less if we're a family by then. Daniel would be working. It still goes, but it's not the centre of my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hollis as long as it lasts, maybe five or six years. We'd marry and buy a house. I'd keep the calligraphy going on the side, for weddings at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd think about it, but my own life seems safe enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Daniel's work when robots come around 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's far away. By then, maybe he'd run his own small firm. I'd trust we'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this that does bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Hollis family, mostly. Mr and Mrs Hollis built that firm. I'd hate to see it go.

say: I'd say people should use ten years to learn **proper trades**.
At church I'd say we should **look after** the young ones.
think: By 2036 I hope to be **a mum**, with my husband working.
My **design job** matters less once we're a family.
do: Stay at the firm **five or six years**.
Keep **calligraphy** going on the side for church weddings.
feel: **Uneasy**, though her **own life** seems safe enough.
S4.quote: By 2036 I hope I'm a mum, and my design job matters less if we're a family by then.
fieldNote: A decade lets **family plans** take priority over career.
Her real grief is for the **owners' firm**, not her own job.
She trusts her husband may **run his own firm** by 2039.

steps.text: Stay at Hollis for five or six years
Marry Daniel and buy a house

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Hollis would close, and we'd have no time to plan the wedding or a house properly. What would help is apprenticeships for young people, paid, in real trades, and firms encouraged to take them on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the small firms. Small family firms like Hollis Print & Design hold a town together. When they go, something goes with them.

headlineQuote: Small family firms like Hollis Print & Design hold a town together.
portrait: Carla is a **junior designer** at a family print firm making invitations and church booklets.
She **never uses AI** and follows her boss's lead in **distrusting** it.
Her fiancé's **electrician work** and her savings steady the household.
She leans on **faith and family** and favours **apprenticeships** over government help.
She's **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, but calmer as timelines lengthen.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when her firm would close with no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** in real trades for young people.
